attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post, stated in the first person.

semantics.note: 'I believe we are on course for' is a firm, unqualified expectation of a crash, so it counts as a forecast. The listed consequences correctly keep 'may' and are not scored. No deadline is stated.

contract.note: Reading 'truly horrible crash' as a broad, severe AI-sector collapse is an ordinary reading. The contract rightly leaves the 'may' consequences out of the test and says continued prosperity cannot disprove an undated prediction.

evidence.note: October 2026 sell-off: hyperscalers down 5.9% and data-center enablers down 18.2% over two weeks. Earnings estimates were barely changed. This shows market stress, not a broad, severe collapse.
Through Q3 2026, AI took over 80% of venture funding while other startups faced selective funding. This shows concentration, not a crash or a restructured venture industry.

reviews.rationale: The firm crash forecast has no deadline. By the cutoff the evidence shows a sharp two-week sell-off and concentrated AI funding, but no broad, severe AI-sector collapse with financing or business disruption. The early-resolution rule is not met. Continued activity cannot contradict an undated forecast, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. He quotes the phrase 'Anthropic actually being profitable on inference' only to reject it.

semantics.note: Calling profitability claims 'fantasy' firmly commits him to the present-tense claim that Anthropic is not profitable on inference. The wording covers the whole company, not just subscriptions.

contract.note: Inference profitability read as serving revenue minus attributable serving costs (gross margin) is the ordinary reading. Q1 2026 is a reasonable choice of the latest completed period. He named no accounting basis, so the reading shapes the result.

evidence.note: The S-1 (an SEC filing published before the cutoff) reports Q1 revenue of $4,731M. Even total compute, including training and free access, was only $3,387M. Cost of revenue for customer-serving work was $2,380M for the whole first half, which caps the Q1 figure. That puts the Q1 serving margin well above zero.

reviews.rationale: The filing gives Q1 2026 revenue of $4,731M. Customer-serving compute costs for the whole first half were $2,380M, and all compute in Q1, including training and free tier, was $3,387M. Any reasonable allocation of serving costs leaves a clearly positive inference gross margin. Only heavy loading of channel fees or overhead, which the ordinary reading excludes, could change that. The claim that Anthropic is not profitable on inference is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter post.

semantics.note: This is a present estimate of how much revenue the development pipeline requires, so observation is the right kind. The 'big problem' part is evaluative and correctly left out of the test.

contract.note: Reading 'substantiate' as covering costs, hardware replacement and a return on capital is ordinary, but he supplied none of the model's inputs. Scope, power basis and revenue layer are all unspecified, so the reading drives the result.

evidence.note: JLL's year-end 2025 report shows a pipeline of roughly 35 GW, which makes 'tens of gigawatts' plausible. It has no revenue model and a different scope and period.
Rystad models required end-user AI spending of about $1T in 2026 and $3.4T in 2030 for hyperscaler capex. That is a different population and revenue layer, so it cannot be matched against $380B.

reviews.rationale: The packet supports a pipeline in the tens of gigawatts but contains no matched model for the same facilities that confirms or refutes roughly $380B a year in required revenue. Rystad's estimates use a different scope and revenue layer and are context only. The evidence does not settle the numerical claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own answer, 'God no', to his own rhetorical question.

semantics.note: 'God no' is a firm, undated denial that Anthropic can take down Figma, so it can be read as a forecast with no deadline. It sits inside a rhetorical point about media credulity, but the commitment itself is firm.

contract.note: Defining 'take down' as business failure or sustained displacement caused by Claude Design is an ordinary reading. Support requires an event that forecloses displacement permanently, which is strict but standard for an undated negative forecast.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own announcement of the Claude Design launch on 2026-04-17. It shows a competing product exists, not that Figma lost ground.
Figma's own disclosure: Q2 2026 revenue up 48% and guidance raised after Claude Design launched. This shows continued strength, not that displacement is foreclosed.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated. Figma kept growing after Claude Design launched, so the claim has not been contradicted. But no dated event permanently rules out displacement, so the early-resolution rule for support is not met either. The claim stays unresolved.
